[{"text": "If you're reading this, I hope it helps navigate the chaos of this place. There's no one to guide you, so it can be quite disorganized. If you're with a group, leave someone in line outside while the rest of you go inside, pick everything you want, and pay at the counter. Then, return outside to wait for a table where your food will eventually be brought to you.

Now, onto the review. This isn't a traditional restaurant it's a fish market that cooks your seafood, offering grilled, fried, and perhaps a few other options. You pick your seafood yourself using plastic bags they provide, and when you're ready, they weigh it and take your name.

We tried several dishes: the salad with feta cheese was excellent, the fried squid was just okay but tasted like old oil, the large shrimp were decent, and the grilled scallops were amazing. I wasn't a big fan of the octopus, but the baked clams were pretty good. The smaller clams in white sauce were okay. We also ordered a red snapper, which they forgot to bring out until we reminded them, so we ended up taking it home.

A few things bothered me. Raw fish was placed near the salad bar, raising concerns about cross-contamination. One worker was cleaning lint out of his phone speaker with a toothpick right by the food, which was off-putting.

[{"text": "Parksanbal is a small, cash-only spot that keeps things incredibly simple , it only serves one dish: Korean beef soup. Your only decision is whether you want it spicy or not spicy. That’s it. And honestly, that’s part of the charm.

The soup itself is rich and comforting. Simmered for hours using beef bones, the broth comes out cloudy and flavorful, with a deep, savory taste. There’s a mix of soft noodles, tender rice, and just a modest amount of meat. While it’s not overloaded with beef, the overall balance of flavors and textures works well. The rice in the broth especially stands out soft, savory, and filling.

Korean beef soup, known as gukbap (국밥), is a soul-warming dish with centuries of history. “Guk” means soup and “bap” means rice, and this meal has long been a staple in Korean households for its heartiness and restorative qualities. The version served at Parksanbal draws from the gomguk or gomtang tradition a milky broth simmered from beef bones for hours (or even days), extracting collagen and marrow to give it that rich, comforting depth.

Alongside the soup, you’ll get a small spread of traditional Korean side dishes: roasted seaweed, a fluffy Korean omelette, ssamjang (a soybean chili paste), Korean hot peppers, and kkakdugi a cubed radish kimchi that adds a nice crunch and tangy kick to the meal.

This dish has deep roots in Korean food culture. Known as gukbap (literally “soup with rice”), it’s a staple comfort food across the country, especially popular in cities like Busan. It’s working-class food in the best way humble, filling, and made with love and patience.

The space is pretty minimal no frills, just a few tables and a calm, unfussy vibe. It’s $20 for the set, which feels reasonable for the portion and overall experience. [{"text": "I don’t normally leave Google reviews. I’m not someone who looks for problems, and I usually go into restaurants without huge expectations, I’m generally easy to please. But what happened today honestly pushed me to write this, and I’m sorry to have to do so.

Today my partner and I went to Wayan and ordered the Restaurant Week menu. We also decided to try the escargot rendang, because we’re always open to new flavors and it sounded great.

For the Restaurant Week menu, we both ordered the same items:

First course: Sate Maranggi

Second course: Chicken Lombok

The escargot rendang, unfortunately, was a complete disaster. It tasted genuinely burnt, overly smoky, with a strong “burnt” flavor, and worst of all it was extremely salty. I truly hope the chef tries it as served (New York location), because it did not taste like a dish that should have left the kitchen.

The Sate Maranggi was the one bright spot, it was tasty and enjoyable, and we ate it happily.

But the worst experience was the Chicken Lombok. There was nothing “wow” about it (it felt like a basic baked chicken in tomato sauce), and on top of that it arrived severely burnt. The burnt taste was impossible to ignore.

As for the drink: my partner ordered a Diet Coke. Honestly, I’m still wondering, did we order a Coke, or just a glass of ice? Because it felt like either the drink was mostly ice, or someone accidentally poured only a small amount of soda into it.

We walked in genuinely excited, especially because my partner is Indonesian, and we left really disappointed. Thanks for the experience (!)", "rating": 2, "author": "Mert Uçar", "published": "a month ago"}, {"text": "Have eaten at their restaurant in Jakarta and now here in New York. [{"text": "Birds of a Feather is one of those rare restaurants that truly delivers on both atmosphere and flavor. From the moment you walk in, the space feels warm, intimate, and thoughtfully designed — a perfect spot for a cozy dinner with friends or a special night out.

The food is the real highlight. Every dish we ordered was beautifully presented and packed with bold, authentic flavors. You can really taste the care and creativity behind each plate. The menu offers a great balance between traditional Sichuan elements and modern twists, making it exciting even if you’ve had Sichuan food many times before. The service was attentive and friendly without being intrusive. The staff were knowledgeable about the menu and happy to give recommendations, which made the experience even better.

Overall, Birds of a Feather is more than just a meal — it’s an experience. If you’re looking for elevated Chinese cuisine in a stylish, welcoming setting, this place is absolutely worth a visit. [{"text": "On my most recent trip to NYC, I checked out Le Crocodile in Williamsburg, had it bookmarked after seeing it on Instagram.

The place was packed, great energy, and overall a solid dinner. That said, it’s not the best French food I’ve had, it leans more toward the middle.

I ordered the duck breast and the roasted chicken. Both were perfectly cooked, no complaints there, but nothing that really stood out or would make me come back specifically for them.

The whole experience felt a bit… short. Good, but not memorable.

In a city like New York with so many standout French spots, this just doesn’t make the cut for a repeat visit.", "rating": 4, "author": "Frank Garcia", "published": "2 days ago"}, {"text": "Delicious:)", "rating": 5, "author": "Izabela Żdan", "published": "6 days ago"}, {"text": "It is one of those rare places that manages to be consistently excellent whether you show up for brunch or dinner. I’ve now done both, and each visit reinforced the same impression: terrific food, genuinely friendly staff, and an atmosphere that makes you want to linger.

Set inside the Wythe Hotel, the space is beautiful—bright, elegant, and lively without feeling overwhelming. It attracts a great mix of people, and there’s an energy in the room that makes it simply a nice place to spend time, whether you’re catching up with friends or settling in for a long meal.

The food absolutely holds up to the setting. The burger is easily one of the best in New York—rich, perfectly cooked, and deeply satisfying. The quiche, though, is what really surprised me: delicate, custardy, and unbelievably flavorful. It’s the kind of dish that sounds simple but ends up being completely mind-blowing when done this well.

And then there’s the sticky toffee pudding. Warm, indulgent, and exactly the kind of dessert you hope for at the end of a great meal.

Between the atmosphere, the hospitality, and the consistently strong cooking, this is a place I keep coming back to.", "rating": 5, "author": "Tim Salikhov", "published": "a week ago"}]

會回訪，下次跟多一點人一起來能吃他們家的signature dish", "rating": 5, "author": "Licht c", "published": "a day ago"}, {"text": "If you’re looking for a fun group dinner spot in NYC, Dag Thai is definitely one to check out 🍜✨

I came here on a Saturday night for a friend’s birthday with a group of 5 and it was perfect for a larger party. Definitely make a reservation though because it gets busy. They have both upstairs and downstairs seating, so there’s a good amount of space which I liked.

We made it just in time for happy hour and I started with the “Be Nice” cocktail 🍸 and wow…SO good. It had this light frothy top and was super smooth. At $15, it felt like a great deal for NYC and I ended up getting two because I loved it that much 😅

Now for the food 👇

We started with the scallop bites which were tasty and a solid appetizer, but not something I’d rush back for.

The Neur Yang (steak) 🥩 was really well done. Cooked perfectly, super flavorful, and came with sticky rice and veggies that balanced it out nicely.

The shrimp fried rice 🍤 was good, but pretty standard nothing super memorable there.

BUT the standout… the Dagg Haeng Noodle 🍜🔥
This was AMAZING. The crispy pork was perfectly done and the noodles were so flavorful. Easily my favorite dish of the night and the one I’d go back for again and again.

We finished with the taro puff which was a nice sweet ending to the meal 🥮

Service wise, everything came out really fast which I appreciated, but I will say they do try to move you along pretty quickly and are strict about the 1.5 hour table time. They also brought out entrees before appetizers which felt a little rushed.

Overall, really good food, great for groups, and a fun vibe for a night out in the city. I’d definitely come back especially for those noodles 🤩", "rating": 5, "author": "Plate Cleaner Club", "published": "a day ago"}]

[{"text": "Best Thai food in NY!! So good and the owner is super sweet too.", "rating": 5, "author": "Haridher Pandiyan", "published": "a year ago"}, {"text": "Shiver Me Thai On Staten Island:

Burrrr - licious !

That's my vibe as I stumbled upon the Thalay Thai restaurant on Staten Island after a snowstorm this year. It's the perfect spot for an Asian winter warrior such as I, to refuel and charge on through the snow storm, with a delicious Thai meal.

I miss Asian food a lot during this time of year. Thalay was a great find, tucked away on Stuyvesant Road. The Thai eatery is walking distance from the Staten Island ferry point. It's run by a (Thai) mum and pop (husband and wife) who are so kind and charming that they are one of my favourite parts of the visit to this restaurant. They ran a similar restaurant in Bangkok, Thailand and then Manhattan and are now located on Staten Island right by the St George Ferry!

It's nothing fancy and a little bit of a hole in the wall spot. But it's clean and brightly lit making it a nice place for a quick bite to eat indoors or take-away stop. .

Some of the things I liked about this restaurant are: the food which is delicious and quite authentic to me as a South East Asian resident for decades. I liked the basil fried rice and pad thai which I selected - both with shrimp! The portions are enormous at this restaurant at least for my little Asian tummy. The prices are so reasonable with a lunch special for USD 13 dollars which includes one main and one mini appetizer. A really good value for money special lunch.

My only point of recommended improvement could be less oil on the fried items like spring rolls and coconut shrimp which I ordered for starters. But a quick tissue to the rescue drenches up the extra oil for this very health conscious eater.

I highly recommend this spot for the kind service, quality of food, authentic Thai taste and value for money.

The frosty draft was the king in Kings County. Imagining the long day ahead, I decided to start with something warm and healthy. Or at least tasty. Okay, just tasty. After all, it was my birthday — I owed myself a treat!

I headed to Bou’ote, one of the most stylish cafés in Central Brooklyn which sticks out like a Monet painting dropped in the middle of Springfield, TN.

The café is run by Shlomo, a tough-looking Israeli guy, likely with a military past, who somehow manages to blend grit and charm in equal measure. Okay, almost equal.

As I sat sipping my coffee, a mailwoman walked in. She was young, sporting a Jamaican accent, and looked like she’d been frozen solid on her route. Yet when offered a cup of coffee, she refused with a smile.

“You made me a coffee yesterday and the day before that. You’re going to spoil me!” she laughed.

Shlomo leaned over the counter, unfazed. “Fine,” he said, “I’ll make you one tomorrow. But today, I need a favor.”

I held my breath, expecting the worst. Asking her to run an errand in this weather? Surely not!

“Are you heading down Troy Avenue?” he asked.

“Yes,” she replied.

“Perfect. Could you take this cappuccino to the school crossing guard? She’s standing out there in the cold all morning — it must be brutal.”

And just like that, my day was made! What I thought would be an awkward feeling turned into the perfect birthday gift: the gift of witnessing kindness, compassion, and care in action.

Shlomo’s gesture was contagious. His cup of coffee warmed two pairs of hands — and who knows how many hearts, mine included. Warmed and inspired.", "rating": 5, "author": "Eli Livshitz", "published": "Edited 10 months ago"}, {"text": "We had a beautiful time at Shlomie’s cafe! The best Georgian cousin in New York!!!", "rating": 5, "author": "Lora Slabodkina", "published": "2 months ago"}, {"text": "One of the best Georgian restaurants in Brooklyn!

We visited Sunny House for my uncle’s birthday celebration in April 2025, and again for my own birthday in September. The first visit was a banquet letting us sample most of the menu. On the second visit, I completed the list. On both occasions the food was consistently fresh, full of flavor, and overall delicious. It’s impressive how they maintain such a high quality across every dish - including dessert and even tea. A few dishes absolutely stood out: Khinkali (both beef and lamb), Megrelian Khachapuri, Adjaruli Khachapuri, Veal Stew (Chashashuli), and Baby Lamb Chops.

The interior is warm and nicely decorated, creating a cozy ambiance. The table setup feels like a proper restaurant, rather than a casual café vibe usual for Georgian spots. The two dining rooms layout allows for some privacy if you host a party. There is nice live music on weekend evenings, but it's very loud. Even in the inner room with doors closed, the music makes it hard to hear each other. If quieter setting to talk and socialize is important - arrive before the music starts.

Service is polite, friendly, and attentive, though it can lag during busy evenings. On non-banquet visit, the entrées arrived immediately after hot appetizers and khachapuri, leaving no time to enjoy the starters while they were still hot. Not sure why it's done that way, probably cultural norm. To have sufficient time to focus on appetizers explicitly ask the staff not to rush the entrees.

I highly recommend Sunny House for its high-quality Georgian cuisine and beautiful, welcoming ambiance!

Dishes tried

Salads & Cold Starters
Georgian salad with Burrata - good
Georgian salad with Walnuts - good
Gebzhalia - delicious! A new dish for me an interesting flavor combo.
Eggplant rolls with walnuts - excellent!
Assorted Pkhali - good.
Satsivi - excellent! Flavorful, fresh, and perfectly textured sauce.
Assorted Smoked Fish

Khachapuri & Breads
Imeruli Khachapuri - excellent, though the Megrelian was even better!
Megrelian Khachapuri - one of the best I ever had! Fresh perfect dough generously filled with cheese inside and on top - truly delicious!
Adjaruli Khachapuri - excellent dough and cheese filling! Only wish they put cheese inside the edges of the boat as well.
Chvishtari (cornbread with cheese) - great.
Fresh Georgian Bread – especially good with sauces like satsivi, shkmeruli, Megrelian Kharcho, Chashashuli.

Hot Starters, Soups & Sides
Lobio - warm and flavorful!
Potatoes with Mushrooms - delicious! A simple dish elevated with garlic, grilled peppers, and fresh herbs.
Grilled mushroom with sulguni cheese - good
Fried Calamari - okay
Soup Kharcho - well -balanced classic kharcho with generous amount of meat. The meat pieces could be larger and fattier for a juicier texture.
Chakapuli - very good and flavorful. Served as a soup here though I've had it as a stew before.

Mains & Grilled Dishes
Khinkali with Beef / with Lamb - this was another hit! Certainly one of the best khinkali I've tried!  Flavorful, well-textured, and full of juice.. Lamb version is quite spicy.
Chicken Shkmeruli - very tasty.
Megrelian Kharcho - excellent! Rich sauce with a bold Georgian spice blend. Same note on meat texture as the regular kharcho.
Veal Stew (Chashashuli) - absolutely amazing! Tender veal that melts in your mouth. The sauce is a magical combo of veggies and Georgian spices creating a unique delicious flavor. I think it’s one of the best dishes at Sunny House.
Lamb Chops - outstanding! Juicy, full of flavor, and cooked perfectly.
Mixed Grill platter (chicken kebab, pork kebab, baby lamb chops, lulya kebab in lavash with grilled peppers) - everything on the platter including grilled peppers was awesome and delicious!
Grilled Trout with Grilled Vegetables - well-prepared and fresh.

Dessert
Napoleon Cake - very fresh and fluffy. The filling didn’t resemble the classic buttery Napoleon, but still enjoyable.", "rating": 5, "author": "beldim2010", "published": "Edited 2 months ago"}]

[{"text": "TL;DR - From a Vietnamese person who has lived in Hà Nội and strongly prefers Northern-style phở over Southern, I was thrilled when a Hà Nội-style shop opened in NYC. I came in here with positive and high expectations, but the long wait, lukewarm broth, and inauthentic flavor left me really disappointed.

High prices ($20 including taxes) and a long wait (about 25 minutes for 1 bowl of phở) despite not a full house, and the worst part was the broth was not even piping hot. My seat mate had to wait about 25 minutes as well, and his broth was also not hot. To illustrate this, the bánh phở (noodles) arrived slightly clumpy and hard, showing that the broth was not hot enough. Phở broth really should be piping hot and this just was not. If they are taking that long with each order, why is the broth not hot? Phở in Việt Nam is served extremely quickly, within 60-90 seconds after ordering. It should not take 25 minutes, particularly for meats that include thịt tái (basically raw meat that cooks in the bowl when served). It is just nonsensical why it takes so long, and other customers from other reviews have also identified these same problems.

The broth is always the most important part of phở. The broth unfortunately is not true to Hà Nội style and is clearly a fusion between Northern and Southern styles. Yes, I know there are some different ways to prepare phở even among HN's most storied and long-running restaurants from Phở Thìn to Lý Quốc Sư, and many more, but the unifying factor is Northern phở should be airy and light, but the broth was fattier than it should have been. The meat they served was too fatty (yes, even for tái gầu) and cut too thick (other people have said this too).

The staff are clearly either from miền Bắc or family members of Northern Vietnamese people, and it pains me that they are serving this under the marketing of authentic northern phở. I know that they know better, and I know that they have the same amazing memories of Hà Nội phở as I do, but it's disappointing that this eatery just cannot come close to reproducing that taste. Obviously, foods prepared in different regions of the world will taste different based on ingredients or staffing, but the recipe they are using just is not cutting it. It just...fell flat considering the expectations that were set up. Spoons were disposable and out of stock at my table so we had to ask for more, but the spoons were tiny and made of plastic -- like to-go spoons. They need to invest in better utensils.

In summary, I really, REALLY wanted to love this place. It was supposed to be a taste of home far from home, but instead I just left disappointed and feeling like I had been fooled. I will say that if you are looking for a warm or 'comforting' bowl of phở, then this will do – but there are cheaper options elsewhere. But if you are coming with the expectations of a reminder of Hà Nội phở, or if you KNOW what Hà Nội phở should taste like, and if you know the taste you expect, I do not think you will find it here. I'm not saying that they are tantalizingly close to the food they promise and market to serve; I would be sympathetic in that case. I am saying that the taste is just not good and really flawed. I

[{"text": "From the moment we walked in to ask about a same-day reservation (we may have just gotten lucky), we knew we had stumbled onto something special. Tucked along Greenpoint Avenue, just a short stroll from Transmitter Park, the location alone sets the tone—but what happens inside is even better.

The vibe strikes that rare balance: intimate and cozy, yet undeniably lively. Even at a 5:45 reservation—with our 4.5-month-old in tow—it felt like a true night out. The room had energy, warmth, and that effortless buzz that makes you want to linger.

The food absolutely blew us away. We ordered a wide range—oysters, Hokkaido milk bread, the newly added five-spice lamb ribs, red snapper sashimi, Japanese sweet potato, wagyu NY strip, and sticky toffee pudding—and not a single dish missed. Every plate was thoughtful, balanced, and memorable in its own way.

The drinks held their own just as much as the food. We tried a mix of cocktails and sake—three sours (two mezcal, one gin), a whiskey cocktail, and a serving of sake—and each one was just as well executed as the last.

What truly sets this place apart, though, is the service. Across the board—from the hostess to the FOH team to management—we felt genuinely cared for. Attentive without being overbearing, warm without feeling scripted—it elevated the entire experience.

And for everything we ordered, the value was honestly shocking in the best way. To have that caliber of food and service, order generously, especially for a Michelin Guide spot—feels almost unheard of.

It’s no surprise they’re on the Michelin Guide, and we’re already wondering how they don’t have a star yet. This will absolutely be in our regular rotation.

If you have the chance to go, don’t hesitate—run, don’t walk.", "rating": 5, "author": "Cassidy-Rae Galos", "published": "2 days ago"}, {"text": "Excellent quality.", "rating": 5, "author": "Andrea G", "published": "2 days ago"}, {"text": "Great restaurant with a creative mix of Japanese and American cuisine. Standout dishes included the Japanese Sweet Potato tempura, Crispy Skin Half Chicken, and the Lingo Beef Pie.

The Tokyo Banana Sundae was a highlight: banana custard, dulce de leche, vanilla ice cream, served in a large glass — delicious and presented interestingly.

The interior is appealing, and the staff is friendly; on our second visit, we were warmly welcomed back by the staff.
However, I noticed that the dinner menu has only one cooked fish option, golden tilefish, which I avoid due to its mercury levels. It would be great to see alternatives like cod or mackerel.", "rating": 4, "author": "Olga NYC", "published": "a week ago"}]

[{"text": "I was really disappointed by my experience at Little Ruby in SoHo today, not because of the food, but because of the service and the way I was treated.

I left my phone number for the waitlist and was told the wait would be about 30 minutes. I stayed nearby for well over that time but never received any text. When I went back to check, a male staff member told me their system showed that a message had already been sent, even though I never received anything. He did eventually seat me, but the situation already felt dismissive.

What made the experience much worse was the service once I was seated. A white female server attended to the neighboring table with warmth — filling water, being friendly, and offering detailed explanations. In contrast, I was simply given water and almost no engagement at all. The difference in treatment was noticeable and uncomfortable. When I asked for takeaway box at the end of my brunch, the same server’s attitude again felt cold and subtly judgmental, reinforcing the sense that I was being treated differently. In addition, I waited for several minutes for her to bring me the check.

After I paid, I stood to wait for the restroom. I may have slightly been in her way, but her reaction was extremely impatient — cold facial expression, visible annoyance, and an overall attitude that felt condescending and unwelcoming.

I rarely write reviews like this, but as a person of color, this experience felt like a microaggression rather than just “bad service.” Respectful and consistent treatment should not depend on who the customer is.

I hope management takes this feedback seriously and reflects on staff training and awareness.", "rating": 1, "author": "Doudou Guo", "published": "3 months ago"}, {"text": "My wife and four teenage children had a late lunch here and it was simply amazing. The place was pretty busy when we went, which usually is a good sign, and the atmosphere felt lively with a steady flow of tables. Service was fine considering how packed it was and the food came out at a reasonable pace. It’s also a Chinese run sushi restaurant, which is very common in New York. Many of these places combine traditional Japanese sushi techniques with modern American style specialty rolls that include sauces, torching, and fried elements.

We started with miso soup, a staple in Japanese cuisine made from fermented soybean paste dissolved into a light dashi broth. Dashi is traditionally made with kombu seaweed and bonito flakes, which gives the soup its deep umami flavor. The soup here was simple with scallions and seaweed and served hot, making it a comforting start to the meal.

For our main dish we ordered the Sashimi Deluxe, which came with 18 pieces of assorted sashimi and a side of sushi rice. The presentation was beautiful, with the sashimi arranged neatly over greens and garnished with pickled ginger, wasabi, and a slice of jalapeño. The assortment included slices of tuna, salmon, and several types of white fish, each cut thick and clean. The tuna had a deep red color and a smooth texture, while the salmon looked bright and slightly fatty, which is what gives salmon sashimi its buttery quality. The sushi rice was served on the side in a neat mound sprinkled with sesame seeds. Proper sushi rice is seasoned with rice vinegar, sugar, and salt, creating a slightly sweet and tangy balance that pairs well with raw fish. Even though the platter looked great and the fish tasted fresh, for the dinner price the portion still felt a little underwhelming. It was good quality but overall not very filling for the amount they charge.

We also ordered several specialty rolls.

The Fire Island Roll was deep fried and very rich. It had salmon, white tuna, kani, avocado, roe, and scallion inside with eel sauce and spicy mayo on top. The frying created a crispy outer layer while the inside stayed soft and creamy from the fish and avocado. The eel sauce added sweetness and the spicy mayo brought a little heat.

The Happy Year Roll had spicy tuna, avocado, and cucumber inside and was topped with torched salmon, roe, scallions, spicy mayo, and eel sauce. Torching the salmon slightly melts the fat in the fish and gives it a light smoky aroma while keeping the inside tender.

The Dancing Tuna Roll had tempura white tuna inside and was topped with pepper tuna, avocado, scallions, tobiko, spicy mayo, and eel sauce. The roll had a lot of texture between the crispy tempura, the soft tuna, and the tobiko which adds small bursts of saltiness.

We also ordered a simple eel avocado roll, which is always a classic combination. The eel is typically grilled and brushed with a sweet soy based glaze known as unagi sauce, which pairs really well with creamy avocado and vinegared sushi rice.

Overall the sushi was good, the fish tasted fresh, and the presentation of the dishes was very nice. The biggest downside for me was the price compared to how filling the meal actually was. Dinner here is definitely on the expensive side for the portion sizes.

They do offer happy hour deals, which might make the experience feel more worth it. Next time I would probably try coming during happy hour instead to see if the value feels a little better.", "rating": 3, "author": "Kimberly Lim Legaspi", "published": "a week ago"}]

[{"text": "Cozy place with great service & delicious food. We ordered crying tiger, spring rolls, chicken satay & massaman curry with roti for appetizers. Mains was chicken basil, drunken noodles, steak basil & salmon bowl. Everything was super delicious & Molly, our server was very friendly, helpful & efficient. Would definitely recommend this restaurant as must try.", "rating": 5, "author": "Sonali Gokhale", "published": "2 months ago"}, {"text": "I was at this unique restaurant a good while ago. As per the name "Isankaya," they are a fun mix of Isan, or Northeastern Thai food, and Japanese izakaya, or bar food. The menu is mostly a mix of dishes from all over Thailand, though only a handful are from Isan.  Otherwise, a handful of them were fusion, and there is a small amount of Japanese dishes. The inside was bright from the red neon, but not too much so, thankfully. The woman serving was very friendly, and while they didn't get too crowded as it was very late when I went, there was still a handful of people there. As it was late, I didn't bother getting a drink, though they do have a small selection of beers along with wine, cocktails, and plenty of soft drinks.

My appetizer was one of the more interesting dishes I had in recent memory. This was the $13.95 E-San Ankimo, with raw monkfish liver in chili lime dressing with cilantro, culantro, shallot, and toasted rice powder. There were 6 reasonably sized pieces of the raw liver with the spice mixture on the bottom and a small amount of greens. If there is a dish on the menu that perfectly represents this restaurant's name, I would say it's this one. The meat on the plate is ankimo, a Japanese delicacy, and the spice mix is what you find commonly in the Isan/Lao version of larb. The dish had a bit of spice, crunch, and a mild amount of heat, which was an interesting pairing to the delicate and slightly fishy and creamy ankimo. This was delicious, and I would go back to get this alone.

I went with one of the few Japanese options as my main dish. This was the Salmon Clay Pot for $28.95, listed as seared salmon served with garlic fried rice topped with fried garlic and ikura. The vessel was presented at the table, and I opened it, revealing the contents. There was plenty of salmon inside, which was buttery and properly cooked. The garlic fried rice had a light crisp to it and plenty of garlic flavor, though some of that was probably from the extra fried garlic. The ikura added some pops of saltiness to this dish. This was also tasty, though I would likely try a Thai dish next time.

I can see why the reviews are so high for this place just from my abridged visit. I would definitely go back.", "rating": 5, "author": "Glenn C", "published": "2 days ago"}, {"text": "Such a great hidden gem for lunch. The space is cozy, aesthetic, and thoughtfully decorated — it has that perfect “hole in the wall” charm while still feeling cute and welcoming.

I ordered the lunch special and got the Thai basil fried rice with shrimp, along with soup and fried chicken, all for around $17, which is an amazing value for the portion size. Everything tasted fresh, flavorful, and well-seasoned.

I also grabbed a Thai iced tea to go for $6, and it was the perfect addition.

The service was attentive and welcoming, which made the experience even better. I didn’t feel rushed at all, which I really appreciated for a solo lunch.

Definitely a spot I’ll be coming back to. Highly recommend if you’re looking for a cozy and affordable Thai lunch.", "rating": 5, "author": "EATWITHEMNYC", "published": "5 days ago"}]
